claims.text: Increasing short-range order in FCC high-entropy alloys increases hardness.
Increasing short-range order in FCC high-entropy alloys increases yield strength.
Short-range order strengthens FCC high-entropy alloys by impeding dislocation motion.
Short-range order produces a higher stacking-fault energy and consequently raises the energy barrier for leading partial-dislocation motion.
Passage of a trailing partial restores the FCC structure but creates a diffuse antiphase boundary by disrupting short-range order on the slip plane.
The energy penalties associated with stacking-fault creation and diffuse antiphase-boundary generation exert back stress on moving dislocations.
Short-range-order-induced resistance to dislocation motion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
At a fixed temperature and strain rate, strength is governed by dislocation-motion-related solid-solution strengthening together with grain-size-dependent Hall-Petch strengthening.
Increasing short-range order changes the Hall-Petch behavior by moving the strongest critical grain size to a smaller value.
Increasing short-range order delays grain-boundary-mediated softening.
Below a sufficiently small grain size, conventional Hall-Petch strengthening breaks down and grain-boundary-mediated softening can occur.
The controlled comparison begins with a single-phase FCC alloy having a random solid solution and minimal pre-existing short-range order.
Controlled annealing or aging can progressively increase short-range order without changing grain size or introducing other relevant microstructural changes.
Extreme temperatures or very high strain rates may activate other deformation modes and cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
The quantitative relationship between short-range-order extent and changes in hardness and yield strength depends on alloy composition and processing.
Electron diffraction or atom-probe tomography can quantify the extent of short-range order for the proposed comparison.

A lack of statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increases at higher measured short-range order, or a lack of the predicted critical-grain-size shift, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experiment holds grain size identical across samples, but the predicted shift in the critical grain size cannot be observed without preparing a grain-size series at each SRO level.

Testing is restricted to grain sizes above the ultrafine or nanocrystalline regime to avoid inverse Hall-Petch behavior, yet the hypothesis also predicts a shift of the strongest size and delayed grain-boundary softening, which generally requires measurements near and across that crossover regime.
